meta.title.home: Freally Teleprompt — look confident, stay on script
hero.sub: A teleprompter for your computer that reads at a real human pace — characters per second, or the BPM of your track — and marks every pause you write into the script.
notice.price: Freally Teleprompt is free today, but it might not be free forever: future versions may be sold.
hero.notice: Version 1.5.0 is the current release. This site has no downloads, and the source code is private.
ladder.title: The road to 2.0
ladder.intro: Every release so far, then the steps planned on the way to 2.0. A step gets its version number when it ships, and a plan can change.
ladder.rung.v0.100.0: The foundation: the app runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, asks you to accept its licence, and scrolls a script with the character-based engine from Freally Capture.
ladder.rung.v0.200.0: The standalone teleprompter: a script library, pause chips, a projector for the talent with a mirror flip, a mirror to phones on your own network, a real transport, BPM pacing and read-aloud.
ladder.rung.v0.300.0: Offline autocomplete: it finishes words and common phrases as you type, in all 18 languages, from word lists inside the app.
ladder.rung.v1.0.0: The first full release: a one-minute welcome tour, a keyboard and screen-reader pass, a theme that follows your system, and updates that install only after you say yes.
ladder.rung.v1.1.0: Write your script by speaking: dictation that runs on your computer, with nothing to train.
ladder.rung.v1.2.0: Dictation, finished: a proper record button, words that land where your cursor is, and an undo that takes back one thing you said.
ladder.rung.v1.3.0: Reading to time: a tempo you tap to match your delivery, a metronome, a bar and beat counter, rehearsal with a timing report, and labels that cost no read time.
ladder.rung.v1.4.0: Getting the script in: import Word, RTF, PDF, text and Markdown files, section markers with a jump list, find and replace, and script statistics.
ladder.rung.v1.5.0: Anything in the room can drive it: foot pedals and presenter remotes, keys that work when the app is not in front, and a rebindable map of every command.
ladder.rung.rig: Built for the rig: a vertical flip for overhead glass, lens and safe-margin guides, an elapsed and remaining time display, and presets for reading at a distance.
ladder.rung.takes: Never lose a take: recovery of unsaved edits after a crash, settings that travel with each script, local version history, and export to PDF for a paper backup.
ladder.rung.writing: Help with the writing: a rhyme finder, syllable counts for each line, a tongue-twister check and suggested pauses — from dictionaries, with no model.
ladder.rung.remote: Drive it from anywhere: a phone-sized control page, plus MIDI and OSC for the desk you already run — on your own network only, and off by default.
ladder.rung.show: Run a whole show: rundowns with a duration for each item, more than one prompter output, and a big countdown and cue-light display for the floor.
ladder.rung.record: Record while you prompt: a webcam take as the script runs, or audio only with your section markers written into the file as chapters.
ladder.rung.languages: Every script, every language: emphasis on single words, furigana above the line, right-to-left polish for Arabic, and vertical Japanese and Chinese.
ladder.rung.v2.0.0: Version 2.0: all of the above, on Windows, macOS and Linux.
ladder.note: Done means released and tagged. Even so, this site offers no downloads.
what.title: What it does
features.pace.title: A real reading pace
features.pace.body: Set the speed in characters per second, or in BPM from 20 to 250 to read in time with a track — not an arbitrary dial from 1 to 10.
features.pauses.title: Pauses you can see
features.pauses.body: Type -- for a short pause or --3 for a three-second hold. Each becomes a chip in the editor, and lights up as the read reaches it.
features.screens.title: Every screen on the same word
features.screens.body: One engine, counted in characters, drives your preview, the talent's projector — flipped for prompter glass if you need it — and phones on your own network, so they never drift apart.
features.import.title: Open the file you were sent
features.import.body: Import Word, RTF, PDF, plain text and Markdown files as clean prompter text, with a report of anything it could not bring across.
features.markers.title: Find your way around
features.markers.body: A line that starts with # becomes a section marker in a jump list, beside find and replace and live word counts.
features.timing.title: Read to time
features.timing.body: Tap your own tempo, hear a click with a count-in, see the bars and beats, and rehearse for a section-by-section timing report.
features.control.title: Pedals, remotes and hotkeys
features.control.body: Every command has a key you can change. Foot pedals and presenter remotes bind like any key, and a key can work even when the app is not in front.
features.writing.title: Help while you write
features.writing.body: Autocomplete in 18 languages from word lists inside the app, and dictation in English: say it, and it is written into the script.
features.private.title: Yours, on your computer
features.private.body: No account, no telemetry, no cloud. Scripts are plain files on your computer, and the app asks the internet one thing: whether a newer version exists.
honest.title: The things most sites put at the bottom
honest.model.title: Dictation uses a speech model
honest.model.body: Dictation is the one part of the app that uses machine learning: Vosk, an open-source speech recogniser, with a small English model of about 40 MB inside the app. It runs on your computer, uploads and downloads nothing, understands English only, and stays off until you switch it on. Everything else is ordinary code and word lists.
honest.update.title: It asks the internet one question
honest.update.body: Each time it starts, the app asks GitHub whether a newer version exists. The request carries no script, no settings and no identifier, and nothing installs unless you say yes. Everything else works with no connection at all.
honest.voice.title: It does not follow your voice
honest.voice.body: Some teleprompters scroll by listening to you read. Freally Teleprompt 1.5.0 scrolls at the pace you set, and you, a key or a pedal take over when the read changes. A voice-following mode was tried in 1.0.0 and removed in 1.1.0.
honest.downloads.title: There are no downloads on this site
honest.downloads.body: No download link, no button and no beta. The source code is private as well.
footer.licence: Proprietary — All Rights Reserved. © Mike Weaver. Free to use today; future versions may be sold. Not open source.
footer.yours: Your scripts are yours. They stay on your computer, and the app's author never receives, stores or relays them.
featuresPage.title: Everything it does
featuresPage.lead: A teleprompter for Windows, macOS and Linux that reads at a real human pace, keeps every screen on the same word, and opens the script you were sent.
featuresPage.version: This page describes Freally Teleprompt 1.5.0, the released version: everything on it is in 1.5.0, and nothing still planned is on it.
featuresPage.numbers.title: By the numbers
featuresPage.numbers.intro: Each figure is what version 1.5.0 does, counted from its code. Nothing is rounded up.
featuresPage.numbers.paces: ways to set the pace: characters per second or BPM
featuresPage.numbers.bpm: BPM: the range it reads to a beat
featuresPage.numbers.formats: kinds of file it imports: Word, RTF, PDF, plain text and Markdown
featuresPage.numbers.systems: operating systems: Windows, macOS and Linux
featuresPage.numbers.languages: languages, in the app and in its autocomplete
featuresPage.numbers.words: words in its autocomplete lists, with 344,891 phrases
featuresPage.numbers.model: speech model, for dictation: on your computer, and off until you switch it on
featuresPage.free.title: Free today
featuresPage.free.body: Everything Freally Teleprompt 1.5.0 does is free today, for everyone: no paid tier, no subscription, no account and no trial that runs out.
featuresPage.cards.title: What version 1.5.0 does
featuresPage.cards.pace.title: A real reading pace
featuresPage.cards.pace.body: Characters per second, or BPM from 20 to 250 for lyrics and verses read to a track. Change either while the script runs and the scroll re-paces at once.
featuresPage.cards.pauses.title: Pause chips
featuresPage.cards.pauses.body: Type -- for a short pause or --N for an N-second hold. Each is one chip the cursor cannot split, it lights up as the read reaches it, and read-aloud turns it into a real silence.
featuresPage.cards.engine.title: Every screen on the same word
featuresPage.cards.engine.body: The preview, the projector and the devices on your network follow one engine, counted in characters, so they agree on the word being read even at different text sizes.
featuresPage.cards.projector.title: A projector for the talent
featuresPage.cards.projector.body: Full screen on any display, mirrored for beam-splitter glass, with its own transport and keys for the person reading.
featuresPage.cards.mirror.title: A mirror to phones and tablets
featuresPage.cards.mirror.body: Off until you switch it on. A link and a QR code open the script in any browser on your own network: read-only, with a key that changes every time the app starts.
featuresPage.cards.import.title: Import Word, RTF, PDF, text and Markdown
featuresPage.cards.import.body: Clean prompter text with its paragraphs kept, and a report that counts what could not come across — pictures, footnotes, comments. Nothing is saved until you say so.
featuresPage.cards.markers.title: Section markers, find and replace
featuresPage.cards.markers.body: A line that starts with # is a marker on the seek bar and in a jump list. Find and replace matches case or whole words, and is undone in one press.
featuresPage.cards.timing.title: Tempo, click and bars
featuresPage.cards.timing.body: Tap your tempo to fit BPM to your own delivery, hear a click with a count-in, and see the bar and beat on screen and as lines on the seek bar.
featuresPage.cards.rehearsal.title: Rehearsal and a timing report
featuresPage.cards.rehearsal.body: Read it through and see each section's planned time against the real one, and the pace you actually read at. It records timings only — no microphone, no audio.
featuresPage.cards.skip.title: Labels that take no time
featuresPage.cards.skip.body: Mark Chorus, [Verse 1] or ## Bridge as words you do not perform: they stay on screen, dimmed, and take no read time, so your lyrics stay on the bar.
featuresPage.cards.control.title: Shortcuts, pedals and hotkeys
featuresPage.cards.control.body: A searchable map of every command, with clashes flagged. Pedals and remotes bind like any key, and a key can work while another app is in front.
featuresPage.cards.writing.title: Autocomplete, dictation and read-aloud
featuresPage.cards.writing.body: Word and phrase suggestions in 18 languages from lists inside the app, dictation in English that runs on your computer, and read-aloud in your system's own voices.
featuresPage.cards.look.title: Your look, your language
featuresPage.cards.look.body: Typeface, size, weight, colour, margins, line spacing and the reading line, on every screen at once. The app speaks 18 languages, in a dark or a light theme.
featuresPage.cards.private.title: No account, no cloud
featuresPage.cards.private.body: Scripts are plain files on your computer, and there is no telemetry. The app's only request to the internet is a check for a newer version, and nothing installs without your yes.
featuresPage.compare.title: Side by side with the commercial teleprompters
featuresPage.compare.intro: Freally Teleprompt 1.5.0 — the released version, the one you can use today — next to six commercial teleprompter apps. Every cell for another product comes from its maker's own pages or app-store listing, checked on 2 October 2026, and prices are in US dollars as of October 2026.
featuresPage.compare.row.systems: Desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux
featuresPage.compare.row.noAccount: Use it without making an account
featuresPage.compare.note.updateCheck: only the update check goes online
featuresPage.compare.note.ourFormats: also RTF, plain text and Markdown
featuresPage.compare.note.wordIos: Word on iPhone and iPad only
featuresPage.compare.row.bpm: Paces the scroll to a music tempo (BPM)
featuresPage.compare.row.pauses: Timed pauses written into the script
featuresPage.compare.row.devices: Shows the script on other devices
featuresPage.compare.note.ownNetwork: on your own network, in a browser
featuresPage.compare.note.btWifi: over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or the internet
featuresPage.compare.note.displayOrLan: a second display, or another device on the network
featuresPage.compare.note.secondMonitor: a second monitor; tablets need other apps
featuresPage.compare.summary: The short version: of these seven, only Freally Teleprompt says it paces the scroll by BPM and holds timed pauses written into the script, and it is the only one that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with no account and no payment.
featuresPage.compare.theyWin: Where they win: PromptSmart, Speakflow and Teleprompter.com scroll by following your voice, and TeleScroll does with a paid add-on; Freally Teleprompt 1.5.0 does not. PromptSmart, Teleprompter.com and Teleprompter Pro have phone and tablet apps that record video while you read and keep your scripts in their cloud, and Speakflow adds AI writing tools and real-time collaboration.
featuresPage.compare.asOf: Freally Teleprompt's column is version 1.5.0, which is released, so the table compares what you can use today. Its price is today's: Freally Teleprompt is free today, and future versions may be sold. The other products change too; this table is as of 2 October 2026.
featuresPage.why.title: Why it is built the way it is
featuresPage.why.engine.title: One engine, counted in characters
featuresPage.why.engine.body: Speed is characters per second, so the preview, the projector and every phone move through the same text at the same rate whatever their font size. The engine is written twice, for the app's core and for its interface, and the two are kept identical.
featuresPage.why.import.title: A converter that says what it dropped
featuresPage.why.import.body: An import counts what it could not bring across instead of losing it quietly, and never turns a typeset dash into a pause nobody wrote.
featuresPage.why.isolate.title: A bad file cannot stop the read
featuresPage.why.isolate.body: Documents are read in a separate process with a time limit, so a damaged PDF ends that one import, not the prompter.
featuresPage.why.local.title: It stays on your machine
featuresPage.why.local.body: No account, no telemetry and no cloud. Your scripts are plain text files you can open in any editor, and the network mirror stays on your own network.
featuresPage.why.consent.title: Nothing happens behind your back
featuresPage.why.consent.body: Settings change only when you press Apply, a key is claimed system-wide only when you ask, and an update installs only after you say yes.
featuresPage.why.keyboard.title: Within reach of the keyboard
featuresPage.why.keyboard.body: Every control has a focus ring, dialogs keep focus inside them, the seek bar is a real slider, and reduced motion and reduced transparency are respected.
featuresPage.coming.title: What is still coming
featuresPage.coming.intro: Stated plainly, because a feature list that hides its gaps is not worth reading. Everything on this page is in 1.5.0; the steps after it are on the road to 2.0, each marked with its state.
featuresPage.coming.ladder: See every step on the road to 2.0
featuresPage.limits.title: What 1.5.0 does not do
featuresPage.limits.voice: It does not scroll by following your voice: you set the pace, and a key or a pedal takes over when the read changes.
featuresPage.limits.dictation: Dictation understands English only; autocomplete and the interface cover all 18 languages.
featuresPage.limits.phone: There is no phone or tablet app: a phone can show the script through the network mirror, read-only, but cannot drive it.
featuresPage.limits.recording: It does not record video or audio while you prompt.
featuresPage.limits.wayland: Under Wayland on Linux, a key set to work while another app is in front may not work, because Wayland does not let apps claim keys system-wide; keys inside the app are not affected.
featuresPage.coming.downloads: There are no downloads on this site, and none on this page.

docs.privacy.title: Privacy and the network
docs.start.p1: Freally Teleprompt is a teleprompter for Windows, macOS and Linux, for presenters, streamers, podcasters, actors, singers and rappers. It opens as one window — your scripts, the editor, the preview and the projector controls — and needs no account.
docs.start.p2: The first time it opens, it shows its licence agreement. Scroll to the end, then choose I Agree, or Decline & Quit. The app cannot be used until you agree; your answer is remembered, and you are asked again only if the agreement changes.
docs.start.p3: A one-minute tour then shows the editor, the pace controls and the projector. Type or paste a script, set your pace and press play.
docs.start.p4: There are no downloads on this site, and the source code is private.
docs.write.p1: Scripts are .ftscript files: plain text in one folder, readable in any text editor. Open Scripts on the toolbar to create, open, rename and delete them. A recent list takes you back to what you were working on, everything is saved as you type, and the app reopens the script you had open last.
docs.write.p2: Type in the editor or paste from anywhere. Under the read-time estimate, a live word and character count shows what you will actually perform — skipped labels and pause marks are not counted — and a warning marks any line long enough to be a whole paragraph.
docs.import.p1: Press Import on the toolbar and choose a Word document (.docx), an RTF, a PDF, a plain text file or a Markdown file. You see the text it produced, and a report, before anything is saved.
docs.import.p2: Paragraphs are kept; bold, fonts and colours are flattened, because a prompter shows one typeface. Curly quotes, long dashes and ellipses become plain ones, and a file saved in an older encoding is read correctly, and the report says so.
docs.import.p3: Pictures, footnotes, comments, headers and footers, link addresses and embedded objects are counted and listed, never dropped quietly. A PDF has no such structure, so for a PDF the report says it could not tell.
docs.import.p4: Name the script — a name is suggested from the file — and press Import. It is added to your library and opened, and it never overwrites a script that already exists. Markdown headings arrive as # lines, so a Markdown script comes with its section markers.
docs.import.p5: A typeset dash becomes an ordinary hyphen, and two of them never turn into a pause, so an imported play does not arrive full of pauses nobody wrote. A text file you wrote with real pause marks keeps them.
docs.find.p1: Press Ctrl+F, or Find on the toolbar, to search the open script. The match count updates as you type; Enter goes to the next match and Shift+Enter to the previous one, wrapping round at both ends.
docs.find.p2: Match case and whole words only narrow the search, and what you type is searched for literally. Replace changes the current match and Replace all changes every one; either is undone with a single Ctrl+Z.
docs.markers.p1: Begin a line with # — # Verse 2, # Q&A, ## Bridge — and it becomes a section marker. Any line that is one of your skip words, such as [Chorus], is a marker too. There is nothing to set up.
docs.markers.p2: Markers appear in a jump list beside the seek bar, which shows the section you are in, and are ruled onto the seek bar itself. Next and Previous walk them; Previous goes to the top of the section you are in first, like a previous-track button. Choosing one moves every screen, the projector included.
docs.pauses.p1: Type -- (a space, two dashes, a space) for a short pause, or --N for a hold of N seconds. Each becomes a chip in the editor: the cursor sits only before or after it, one Backspace removes it, and Shift with an arrow key selects it whole. Set the length of a plain -- under Settings → Reading.
docs.pauses.p2: Copy and paste carry chips intact, and pasted text has its spacing tidied so every pause lands as a clean chip. While the script plays, each pause lights up as the read reaches it and the scroll holds for its length — on the preview, the projector and the network mirror alike.
docs.pacing.p1: Set the speed in characters per second: a real reading rate that every screen follows, whatever its font size. Or switch to BPM, from 20 to 250, to read lyrics and verses in time with a track.
docs.pacing.p2: Both drive the same engine, and changing either while the script runs re-paces it at once.
docs.tempo.p1: A tempo becomes a reading speed through one number: how many characters you read in a beat. Under Settings → Timing → Your own tempo, press Tap three times or more at the tempo you perform at, then choose Use this tempo; Back to the default undoes it. The BPM box then offers only the tempos the engine can reach.
docs.tempo.p2: With BPM on, or the click switched on, the bar and beat appear above the seek bar and bar lines are ruled onto it. Set the beats in a bar, from 2 to 12, under Settings → Timing.
docs.tempo.p3: Tick Play a click at the current tempo for a quiet tick on every beat, higher on the first beat of each bar; the start countdown becomes its count-in. The app makes the sound itself and times every tick against the audio clock, so it does not drift. It stays silent while read-aloud is speaking.
docs.rehearsal.p1: Tick Rehearse, and time my read under the transport, press play and read aloud as you would on the day. Pause, go back, change the speed: all of it is part of the measurement.
docs.rehearsal.p2: Untick it and the rehearsal report opens: one row per section, with the time it should have taken at your pace, the time it took and the difference. Sections are your paragraphs, or your section markers when the script is divided by them. If you read at a different pace, the report offers that speed, and one click applies it.
docs.rehearsal.p3: While you rehearse, a quiet warning appears once the read is three seconds or more behind or ahead of its plan. Rehearsal records timings and nothing else: it opens no microphone and keeps no audio, and it cannot run together with read-aloud.
docs.skip.p1: Section labels — Chorus, Verse 2, Bridge — are landmarks you see coming but never say. List them under Settings → Timing → Words you do not perform, one per line. The list starts empty, because it changes how a script is timed.
docs.skip.p2: A line that is nothing but a label is skipped whole: brackets, hashes, a colon and a trailing number are seen through, so Chorus, [Verse 1], ## Bridge and Chorus: all match. The same word inside a real line skips only itself. Matching ignores capitals and only matches whole words.
docs.skip.p3: Skipped text stays on screen, dimmed, so the talent still sees it coming, and read-aloud never says it. Because a label takes no time, the scroll passes it at once — and your lyrics stay on the bar you wrote them for.
docs.playback.p1: Play, pause, stop, rewind and fast-forward are on-screen buttons; hold rewind or fast-forward to keep going. Spin the mouse wheel to scrub, click a word to start from it, or hover over the seek bar to see the words at that point.
docs.playback.p2: The seek bar shows the elapsed and total read time, pauses included. A reading guide keeps the current word on the reading line, and the last lit word never scrolls out of sight.
docs.shortcuts.p1: Open Shortcuts on the toolbar. Press the binding you want to change, then press the key, remote or pedal you want; Escape leaves it as it was. Search by a command's name or by the key itself. If two commands share a key, both rows say so; clear one with ×, or choose Restore defaults.
docs.shortcuts.p2: Most foot pedals and presenter remotes send ordinary keys, usually F13 to F24, so they bind with no driver and no setup. Bindings follow the physical key, not the letter printed on it, so they survive a change of keyboard layout.
docs.shortcuts.p3: The Anywhere column asks your system to deliver a key even when another app is in front — a camera app, a DAW or OBS. Nothing is claimed until you set it, and a key another program already owns says so. Under Wayland on Linux, apps cannot claim keys system-wide, and the dialog tells you.
docs.shortcuts.p4: While you are writing, the space bar, the arrow keys and Home type as normal: a bare key runs its command only outside the editor.
docs.countdown.p1: Set Countdown before starting under Settings → Reading, and pressing play counts down that many seconds first, on the preview and the projector, so the talent has a moment before the first word moves. With the click on, the countdown is also the count-in.
docs.projector.p1: Press Projector and choose the display the talent reads from: the script fills that screen edge to edge. Turn on the mirror for beam-splitter glass, where the reflection would otherwise read backwards. The projector has its own transport, seek bar and keys for the person reading.
docs.projector.p2: The preview and the projector lay the script out at the same width and scale it to fit, so they break lines in the same places. Check that the mirrored text reads correctly through your own glass before a shoot.
docs.mirror.p1: To show the script on a phone, tablet or second laptop, open Settings → Network → Mirror to my network and tick Mirror the script to devices on my network. Tick Allow other devices, not just this computer as well — without it, the mirror answers only on this computer — and press Apply. A link and a QR code appear: scan the code, or open the link in a browser on the same network.
docs.mirror.p2: The mirror follows the same engine, so every device is on the same word as the operator. Each device sets its own text size with A− and A+ without changing anyone else's screen.
docs.mirror.p3: The page is served by the app itself, straight to your devices — never through this website, which a browser would not let reach a device on your network anyway. It is read-only: no browser can start, stop, seek or edit anything. Its link carries a key that changes every time the app starts. It is plain HTTP, so the key is not encrypted on the way: use it on a network you trust, not on public Wi-Fi.
docs.mirror.p4: If a device cannot connect: check both switches; make sure it is on the same network, not on mobile data or a guest network that keeps devices apart; allow the app through your firewall for private networks when your system asks; and if Settings says the mirror could not start, change the port and press Apply again.
docs.readAloud.p1: Tick Read aloud with per-OS speech synthesis to hear the script in your system's own voices: Windows OneCore or SAPI, macOS AVSpeechSynthesis, or Speech Dispatcher or espeak-ng on Linux. No voice is bundled with the app.
docs.readAloud.p2: The transport, the seek bar and a click on a word drive the speech, and the highlight follows it — word by word where the system reports word boundaries, at your pace elsewhere. Pauses become short silences, and -- is never read out as "dash".
docs.readAloud.p3: Read-aloud is for the preview only: it never moves the projector. The checkbox is locked while a read is playing or paused, until you press Stop. Check that it speaks on the computer you will present from, especially on Linux.
docs.autocomplete.p1: As you write, the rest of the word appears dimmed ahead of the cursor; finish a word and press space, and it can offer a whole common phrase. Tab accepts, Esc dismisses, and typing on ignores it.
docs.autocomplete.p2: Each of the 18 languages has its own word and phrase lists — 463,985 words and 344,891 phrases in all — inside the app, and only the language you write in is loaded. Under Settings → Editor, turn it on or off and choose its language, which can differ from the app's.
docs.autocomplete.p3: The lists are built from the Tatoeba sentence collection (CC BY 2.0 FR), credited in the NOTICE file that comes with the app. It is a dictionary lookup — instant, predictable and offline, with no model.
docs.dictation.p1: Open Settings → Voice, tick Write my script by speaking and press Apply. A round record button appears above the script: press it and talk, and what you say is written where your cursor is. Press it again to stop; the microphone is open only in between.
docs.dictation.p2: Dictated text is ordinary script text, and Ctrl+Z takes back one thing you said, not the whole session. Expect to tidy punctuation and names: it is a quick way to a draft, not a finished script.
docs.dictation.p3: Dictation understands English only. It uses Vosk, an open-source speech recogniser, with a small English speech model — a trained neural network of about 40 MB — that ships inside the app. It runs on your computer, works with no connection, uploads and downloads nothing, and saves nothing but the text you see. It is off until you switch it on. If the script is mirrored to your network, dictated words reach those devices as they are written, like typing.
docs.settings.p1: Under Settings → Appearance, set the typeface, weight and text colour, the side margins, the line spacing and where the reading guide sits; the font size is under Reading. They apply to the preview, the projector and the network mirror together.
docs.settings.p2: Settings work on a draft: nothing changes until you press Apply, and Cancel restores what you had. Choose one of 18 languages, or Same as my system. The theme is Dark, Light or Same as my system; the reading surface stays high-contrast whichever you choose.
docs.settings.p3: With Minimize to the system tray on, under Settings → General, minimising puts the app in the tray instead of the taskbar. Show the tour again, also under General, replays the welcome tour.
docs.access.p1: The first time the app opens, after the licence, a four-step tour shows the editor and its pause marks, the pace controls and the projector. Skip, Esc or a click outside it closes it for good; Settings → General → Show the tour again brings it back.
docs.access.p2: Every control shows a focus ring when you reach it from the keyboard. Tab stays inside an open dialog, Esc closes it, and focus returns to the button that opened it. The seek bar is a real slider: the arrow keys move one character, Page Up and Page Down a screenful, and Home and End go to either end.
docs.access.p3: If your system asks for reduced motion, animations and blur are dropped while the script itself still scrolls; with reduced transparency, dialogs dim the background instead of blurring it.
docs.problems.p1: When something goes wrong that the app can tell you about, its message has a Report button beside it. After a crash, the next launch shows a strip with Report and Dismiss.
docs.problems.p2: Report opens the Freally Teleprompt report page in your browser, with the technical details already filled in: you can read them, but not change them. Add what you were doing and, if you like, an email address. Nothing is sent unless you press Send on that page, and nothing is ever sent in the background.
docs.problems.p3: Once per launch, the app asks GitHub whether a newer version exists. If there is one, you see its version number and release notes and choose yes or no; an update is checked against a signing key inside the app before it installs. When you are offline or already up to date, it says nothing. Check for updates on the toolbar asks again at any time.
docs.privacy.p1: No account and no telemetry. Your scripts are .ftscript files on your computer, where you save them, and the app's author never receives them.
docs.privacy.p2: The only request the app makes to the internet is the update check, which sends no script, no settings and no identifier. A problem report leaves only from the report page in your browser, when you press Send. The projector and the network mirror stay on your own displays and your own network.
docs.privacy.p3: Machine learning is used in one place: dictation's speech model, which runs on your computer and is off until you switch it on. Autocomplete is a dictionary lookup, read-aloud uses your system's own voices, and nothing you type or say is sent to an AI service.
